title: Beatrix and the Locker
premise: Odile Winterbourne, debate champion and master of deflection, has spent years perfecting the art of 'fine' — until notes signed by the school's legendary ghost, the Locker Wraith, begin appearing in their locker, written in ink that vanishes by morning and knows things Odile never told anyone. As Odile investigates, they discover the ghost is tied to a student erased from school history decades ago, and that the current principal built her reputation on that erasure. Winning the state championship becomes Odile's only leverage to force the truth into the open — but exposing it means betraying the friends whose families are implicated. In the end, Odile loses the championship on purpose, reads the ghost's final letter aloud at prom, and wins something better: a school that finally says the erased student's name.
about_author: Orsen Eriksen is the pen name of a former high-school debater who spent four years arguing about things that didn't matter while ignoring the ones that did. They write stories about kids who are excellent at words and terrible at honesty.

chapters.title: Fine
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. We open mid-debate: Odile dismantles an opponent effortlessly, then comes home to a mother who rewrites every conversation and a father who's stopped trying. Establishes Odile's armor — wit, achievement, invisibility. Emotional beat: competence as camouflage; the reader sees the crack before Odile does.

chapters.title: The First Note
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. A note in the locker: 'You're not fine, Odile.' The ink fades by lunch; no one else saw anything. Odile assumes a prank and prepares a counterattack, cataloguing suspects with forensic delight. Emotional beat: irritation masking fear — someone has seen through them, and being seen feels like danger.

chapters.title: Impossible Ink
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Priya, Odile's lab partner, who tests a confiscated note and finds no known compound. The notes continue, each more personal, referencing a fight Odile had alone in the stairwell. Odile and Priya form an uneasy alliance. Emotional beat: reluctant intimacy — investigation as an excuse to be known.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Wasn't Here
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The notes name someone: 'Ask about Marguerite Voss, class of 1974.' Yearbooks have her photo razored out; teachers go quiet. Principal Halloway catches Odile digging and offers a scholarship threat wrapped in kindness. Emotional beat: first real fear of power — the adult world closes ranks.

chapters.title: Debate Season
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Championship pressure mounts; Odile channels everything into winning, becoming ruthless with teammates, including loyal best friend Marcus, whose grandfather was on the 1974 student council. A note appears in Marcus's locker too. Emotional beat: loyalty strained — Odile is becoming what they're fighting.

chapters.title: What Marcus Knew
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. He confesses: his family archive holds letters proving Marguerite was expelled after accusing a beloved teacher — Halloway's mentor — and died within the year. He's been silent to protect his grandfather's legacy. Emotional beat: the cost of loyalty; two truths that cannot both be kept.

chapters.title: The Locker Opens
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Following the notes' clues, Odile opens the sealed old locker at midnight and finds Marguerite's journal — and realizes the 'ghost' is Ms. Ferro, the retiring librarian who was Marguerite's friend, still keeping a promise. Emotional beat: grief and relief — the mystery resolves into a human debt unpaid for fifty years.

chapters.title: The Argument at Home
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile finally has the argument they could never win — confronting their mother, who reveals she knew about Marguerite (Halloway is her old classmate) and chose silence to survive. Odile refuses to inherit that choice. Emotional beat: rupture as liberation; 'fine' dies here.

chapters.title: Championship
chapters.summary: Priya and Marcus POV, alternating. At states, Odile reaches the final round, where the assigned topic eerily mirrors the cover-up. Instead of the prepared case, Odile argues Marguerite's story before judges, cameras, and a horrified Halloway — forfeiting the title. Emotional beat: climax; losing loudly as the only way to win.

chapters.title: Prom, With Names
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The recording spreads; an inquiry opens; Halloway resigns. At prom, Odile reads Marguerite's last letter aloud as Ms. Ferro watches, and the school dedicates the library to her. Marcus stays; Priya stays; home remains hard but honest. Final note in the locker: 'Thank you, Odile.' Emotional beat: belonging earned not by invisibility but by voice.
